commit: 79837f3 (round 1, incomplete) + ce13a5b (round 2, landed) fix(menubar): re-anchor attention bubble during drag
problem: Dragging the floating pet (Maew) while an attention bubble is displayed detaches the bubble: it stays pinned at its old anchor instead of tracking the pet during the drag.
solution: Round 1 (79837f3, INCOMPLETE) re-anchored the bubble via frameChangeHandler — but that handler fires only on mouseUp, because state persistence is deliberately deferred off the per-tick drag path for perf (phase-04). So the bubble only snapped back at drag END. Round 2 (ce13a5b, LANDED) adds a separate liveFrameChangeHandler fired from applyPanelFrame on every mouseDragged/resize tick doing a cheap in-memory bubble re-anchor; persistence stays on mouseUp. Do not collapse the two handlers back into one — the live (per-tick, no I/O) and committed (mouseUp, persists) paths have different cost budgets.
prompt_lesson: Two transferable lessons. (1) For any draggable/resizable container, enumerate every child or attached overlay (bubbles, badges, affordances, pills) and assert each tracks the same transform — coordinate-space cohesion is the UI analogue of cross-file-atomicity. (2) The round-1 miss is its own class: chrome re-anchoring must hook the LIVE per-tick move path, not a persisted-on-mouseUp handler. A perf optimization that defers state writes off the drag hot path will silently starve any overlay that piggybacks on the persist callback. When you see a deferred/debounced commit path, ask what else needed the high-frequency signal it dropped. Reachability caveat: only review-reachable when container drag-handler + overlay live in the same ticket diff; here pet (P4) and bubble (P6) shipped in different phases, so per-ticket review saw neither pair — integration-of-features bugs need a phase-level review pass.
test_reachability: Weak. Integration behavior: a real NSPanel drag emitting per-tick frame moves while an AttentionBubblePanel is live. BubbleLayout.frame is a pure function and was already correct; the regression was the missing *call* on the live drag path. FloatingPetPanelSpy (controller tests) does not exercise it. Verified by build + manual drag QA across both rounds — round 1 passed build but failed manual QA, which is exactly why ledger lines are written at verified-commit time, not on first green build.
rounds_note: Round 1 was committed+recorded prematurely (as rounds:1) before human verification and proved incomplete. Folded into one entry rather than codogotchi-02 — same bug, same gap. Methodology takeaway: when a fix does not one-shot, instrument critical paths with debug logging to find the real signal flow before guessing again (here: logging would have shown frameChangeHandler firing only on mouseUp).

problem: The Focus button in the attention bubble (1) always focused a hardcoded IDE app regardless of where the hook actually fired from, and (2) could not distinguish between VS Code forks (Cursor, Insiders, Antigravity) or reach Zed/VS Code Insiders/Antigravity embedded terminals at all. Standalone terminals (Warp, Ghostty, Terminal.app) were unreachable. Codex Desktop was misidentified as claude_code due to PascalCase event name collision.
solution: Four-layer fix: (1) CODOGOTCHI_ORIGIN=codex env var injected into Codex Desktop hook command to override PascalCase heuristic; (2) detectTerminalBundleId() in hook-binary.ts detects parent terminal from well-known env vars and writes terminal_bundle_id into source_event in state.json; (3) __CFBundleIdentifier fallback catches any IDE that directly spawns a shell without login intermediary — confirmed working for VS Code Insiders, Antigravity, Zed; (4) Focus button priority: terminal_bundle_id first → IDE-native origin map (cursor, codex) → no-op. Round 1 shipped correct architecture but missed IDE embedded terminals. Round 2 added Zed (ZED_TERM), __CFBundleIdentifier VS Code fork disambiguation, and __CFBundleIdentifier catch-all. Debug dump (CODOGOTCHI_DEBUG_TERMINAL=1 codogotchi-hook) used to validate each terminal, then stripped.
prompt_lesson: The Focus button was specified against a fixed origin→app map. No ticket asked 'what app should Focus target when origin=claude_code running in a terminal?' — the spec assumed a 1:1 mapping that doesn't exist for CLI tools. Lesson: for any user-facing action that targets an external app, the spec must enumerate the CLI-vs-IDE distinction and the embedded-terminal case explicitly. A reviewer reading the phase-06 tickets had no way to flag this because the gap was in the requirements, not the implementation.
test_reachability: None — terminal detection requires real process spawn chains. Unit-testable in isolation (detectTerminalBundleId is a pure function of env), but the end-to-end path (IDE spawns shell → hook fires → state.json written → bubble reads it → Focus tapped) is integration-only. The pure function is exported and testable; integration is verified by CODOGOTCHI_DEBUG_TERMINAL=1 spot-checks.

commit: 000375f feat(soa): append gate transition telemetry log
problem: The direct SoA gate sidecar only preserved the resident last-write-wins `gate.json` payload. Once a ticket moved through multiple gates, there was no durable record of which gates fired for that ticket or what `{ since, expires_at }` window was emitted for each one, which blocked empirical TTL tuning and post-hoc inspection.
solution: Keep `gate.json` as the renderer input, but append every emitted gate payload to `$CODOGOTCHI_HOME/gate-transitions.log` as one JSON line with the same `{ gate, since, expires_at, plan_key, ticket_id }` shape. This preserves transition order and the exact TTL window written for each emission without changing render behavior. Do not try to reconstruct history from resident `gate.json`; the append-only log is the audit trail.
prompt_lesson: When a feature intentionally uses an ephemeral last-write-wins sidecar for live behavior, ask separately whether operators also need a history lane for tuning and diagnosis. Current-state transport and observability history are different products.
test_reachability: Good. Cheap automated coverage can assert that every `writeGateEvent` call appends one line to `gate-transitions.log`, and multi-transition flows can assert ordering (`ticket_completed` before `ticket_started` in cook-mode advance). End-to-end behavior was also verified by simulating a full ticket gate sequence and by empirical confirmation that TTL still limits rendered gate lifetimes correctly.

commit: 983bd28 fix(menubar): scale gate badges with floating pet
problem: The floating SoA gate badges stayed at a fixed visual size while the floating pet itself resized, so shrinking or enlarging the pet broke the chrome-to-pet proportion and made the badges look detached from the transformed frame.
solution: Derive gate badge metrics from the floating pet frame width instead of hardcoding them. Padding, badge height, corner radius, inter-badge spacing, and font size now scale with the pet width and clamp to a minimum so tiny pets do not collapse. The badge panel continues to remeasure during reposition, so drag/resize keeps the scaled chrome anchored correctly.
prompt_lesson: When a ticket adds chrome attached to a resizable surface, the spec must say whether that chrome is fixed-size or scales with the host. Anchoring alone is not enough; transform behavior is a separate requirement that should be spelled out and reviewed explicitly.
test_reachability: Good for automated layout math, limited for final aesthetics. Pure tests can assert that larger pet widths produce larger badge metrics and that very small widths clamp at a minimum scale, which now exists in controller coverage. Final acceptance still benefits from visual QA because proportional correctness is partly perceptual.

commit: ae4da1b feat(menubar): log tool_command and reason_kind in transition log + cad7526 fix(hook): classify ci scripts as testing
problem: state.json already carried tool_command (the raw Bash/Shell command the producer classified) and attention.reason_kind, but state-transitions.log recorded only ts/state/prev/source_origin/source_kind/source_name. state.json is a single last-write-wins snapshot overwritten on every event, so the only durable, append-only record was missing exactly the fields needed to audit producer-side behavior after the fact. This was caught by spotting live in state.json that `bun run ci` was being bucketed as the generic `implementing` fallback instead of `testing` — a misclassification that would have been invisible from the durable log because the command that drove a transition was never recorded. The reason_kind gap is the same shape: standby and errored both gate the attention bubble but the log could not say which attention path fired.
solution: Add tool_command and reason_kind to the transition-log NDJSON line. Decode tool_command in StateJsonReader (reason_kind was already decoded into AttentionPayload.reasonKind), thread both through StateSnapshot, and emit them in TransitionLog.LinePayload via encodeIfPresent so they are omitted on non-shell transitions and heartbeats. The linked-but-separate heuristic defect (`bun run ci` and siblings missing from TEST_RUNNER_PREFIXES) was patched directly in the same pass: ci-family scripts now classify as testing; the word-boundary matcher treats `:` as a stop so ci:quiet needs its own prefix entry.
prompt_lesson: When a producer enriches a live last-write-wins snapshot with new diagnostic fields (here tool_command and attention.reason_kind), the matching append-only audit log must be updated in lockstep or the enrichment is only observable by watching the snapshot at the right millisecond. Current-state transport and observability history are different products and drift apart silently. A second lesson surfaced from the same gap: heuristic classifiers (TEST_RUNNER_PREFIXES) are only auditable retroactively if the input that drove each classification is itself logged — otherwise misroutes like `bun run ci`->implementing are pure luck to catch.
test_reachability: Good. TransitionLogTests now asserts both fields appear when present and are omitted when absent; the existing source-field-omission test covers the lean-line contract. hook-binary tests cover the ci-family classification. Known coverage limit (documented, not yet closed): transition lines fire only on state change, so a command that does not change state is still not logged at all — full command-level auditing would need per-event logging, deliberately deferred for volume/rotation cost.

commit: aa0ac3a fix(test): stop router-help-trim setup test from clobbering real IDE config
problem: Codex Desktop telemetry silently vanished from ~/.codogotchi/state-transitions.log after 2026-05-31T16:26:03Z (no codex-origin lines thereafter), while claude_code lines continued. Initial hypothesis was that Codex was bridging to the claude_code origin via the PascalCase heuristic. That was wrong: CODOGOTCHI_ORIGIN=codex was still correctly set in ~/.codex/hooks.json. The real cause: the bare-dispatch reachability tests in router-help-trim.test.ts set CODOGOTCHI_HOME to /tmp/nonexistent-${Date.now()} but did NOT set CODOGOTCHI_USER_ROOT. installHooks resolves IDE-config paths via getUserRoot() (CODOGOTCHI_USER_ROOT or homedir()), NOT CODOGOTCHI_HOME, so on a fresh sandbox home `setup` ran to completion and rewrote the developer's REAL ~/.codex/hooks.json and ~/.codex/hooks/codogotchi.toml, baking CODOGOTCHI_HOME=/tmp/nonexistent into the hook command. Codex then wrote its state to a throwaway /tmp dir that never existed for the renderer. Every `bun test`/`bun run ci` re-corrupted it — and because the SoA review subagent for phase 08 was run via codex-cli, running the suite broke Codex's own hooks (a self-inflicted feedback loop). ~/.cursor/hooks.json and ~/.claude/settings.json were untouched (Cursor uses a separate installer the bare setup did not trigger; Claude hooks omit CODOGOTCHI_HOME entirely).
solution: Sandbox BOTH CODOGOTCHI_HOME and CODOGOTCHI_USER_ROOT to fresh temp dirs in the offending tests, and seed config.json in the home so `setup` short-circuits on ConfigExistsError (exit 2) before reaching the install step at all — side-effect-free. Relaxed the fictional `exits 2 with missing-config` premise (a fresh home never hit that path; the test only passed before because install succeeded against the real fs). Verified the full CLI suite no longer changes ~/.codex/hooks.json (hash + backup-count unchanged across a run). Then repaired the live ~/.codex/hooks.json and codogotchi.toml back to the real home. Other setup-dispatching tests (rpg, setup) were already safe because they inject a fake installHooks via DI.
defect_class: NEW: test escapes sandbox and mutates real user dotfiles
prompt_lesson: State sandboxing (CODOGOTCHI_HOME) and config-target sandboxing (CODOGOTCHI_USER_ROOT) are two independent isolation boundaries; a test that overrides only one can let a real install routine write the developer's actual ~/.codex/~/.cursor. Any test that dispatches a command capable of filesystem installs must either inject a fake installer (DI, as rpg/setup tests do) or sandbox EVERY root the install resolves. A reachability test should never reach a destructive side effect — seed state so it short-circuits. Bonus systemic lesson: when an agent platform (codex-cli) is used as the review subagent and that review runs the test suite, a sandbox-escaping test can sabotage that very platform's integration, masquerading as a platform bug.
test_reachability: Good and now self-guarding. The fix is verified by asserting the real ~/.codex/hooks.json hash and backup count are unchanged after a full `bun test packages/cli` run. A stricter future guard could make the installer refuse to write IDE configs when CODOGOTCHI_HOME points under a /tmp sandbox, as defense-in-depth.

commit: fac4ec0 fix(soa-gate): shorten gate animation TTL from 3min to 30s
problem: The SoA direct-gate sidecar (.son-of-anton/tools/delivery/codogotchi-gate.ts) wrote gate.json with a flat 3-minute TTL (GATE_TTL_MS = 180_000). The renderer uses expires_at to time-box the gate floor animation. Once the persistent floating UI gate badges shipped (phase 08), the long animation TTL became redundant: the badges already tell the user which gate is active, so holding the gate animation for 3 minutes over-rode normal activity-state animation far longer than needed and lagged behind the real workflow.
solution: Drop the flat TTL to 30 seconds (GATE_TTL_MS = 30_000) so the gate.json animation only marks the transition briefly while the badge carries the durable 'which gate is active' signal. Updated the p17-01 TTL assertion (180_000 -> 30_000) and the AGENTS.soa.md contract note. CAVEAT recorded for follow-up: this file lives in the vendored .son-of-anton git subtree, so the change is local-only and the next `/soa update` subtree merge from cesarnml/son-of-anton will revert it unless the same change lands upstream. The durable fix is an upstream son-of-anton commit; this consumer-side edit is a stopgap.
prompt_lesson: When a new always-on UI affordance (the gate badges) supersedes a transient signal (the timed gate animation), revisit the older signal's tuning — it was sized for a world where it was the ONLY indicator. A second, process lesson: behavior constants that live in a vendored subtree need their durable home identified at change time, or the fix silently regresses on the next vendor sync.
test_reachability: Good. p17-01.test.ts pins the exact TTL delta (expires_at - since === 30_000) and passes. Note the subtree's own test suite is NOT part of codogotchi's `bun run test` (which is `bun test packages convex`), so this assertion only runs when the subtree tests are invoked directly or upstream.

commit: 52d156c feat(menubar): add animation badge on floating pet
problem: The floating pet showed gate UI badges (which SoA gate is active) but had no always-on indicator of the underlying activity-state animation the pet was currently playing. A user watching the pet could not read at a glance whether it was Coding, Testing, Thinking, etc. — the animation itself was the only signal, which is ambiguous across visually similar states.
solution: Added a persistent animation badge in the same spirit as the gate badges. Anchored bottom-left INSIDE the floating pet frame (bottom and left edges sit one inset inside the border, contrasting the gate badge which sits above the top border), and scales with the pet frame by reusing GateBadgeLayout.metrics as the single scaling source of truth. The badge is driven by FloatingPetPanelController.apply(state:) so it tracks the live animation, is shown whenever the pet is visible, and re-anchors on every drag/resize tick alongside the existing chrome. Added ActivityState.displayLabel with concise human-readable copy for all 19 states; the four review-family gate states are deliberately disambiguated (Adv Review / Polling / Recording / Review Clean) since their raw names are confusable. The badge panel ignores mouse events and anchors bottom-left, so it never collides with the bottom-right resize affordance or intercepts drags.
prompt_lesson: When a surface already carries one machine-readable signal as chrome (gate badges) but the primary signal (the animation) is only legible to someone who already knows the sprite vocabulary, a human-readable label closes the gap cheaply. Design choice worth stating explicitly in the spec: where multiple chrome elements attach to the same resizable frame, assign each a distinct corner/edge so anchoring rules never fight (gate badge = top-outside, attention bubble = below, animation badge = bottom-left-inside, resize affordance = bottom-right-inside).
test_reachability: Good. AnimationBadgeLayout.frame anchoring (bottom-left inside) and visible-frame clamping are unit-tested; metrics scaling is asserted to share the gate badge source of truth; ActivityState.displayLabel is tested for non-empty, concise (<=14 chars), and unique labels across all 19 cases. Final aesthetics (exact inset feel, legibility over the sprite) still benefit from a visual spot-check.

problem: The codogotchi-lite spritesheet reserved rows 1 and 2 for idle-impatient / idle-frustrated, with RowSpec constants (idleImpatientLiteRow / idleFrustratedLiteRow) and a doc comment saying they are 'renderer-selected based on elapsed-idle thresholds' — but nothing referenced them. The renderer had no elapsed-idle timer and no row-selection logic, so the prepared art was dead and the pet never escalated while the user was away. A QA request to 'test the transition idle -> idle_impatient -> idle_frustrated' surfaced that the behavior did not exist.
solution: Implemented the renderer-side escalation in FloatingPetScene. While the agent stays continuously idle, the scene walks idle -> impatient (5 min) -> frustrated (10 min) and holds frustrated until the next state transition resets it (last_until_next_transition). idle_impatient/idle_frustrated are deliberately NOT ActivityState cases — they are renderer-internal variants of idle, so there are zero producer/state.json/enum changes. Thresholds live in IdleEscalationConfig (production 5min/10min) and are overridable from the environment for fast manual testing (CODOGOTCHI_IDLE_IMPATIENT_MS / CODOGOTCHI_IDLE_FRUSTRATED_MS, milliseconds). The scene owns escalation (injected clock + config, recomputed on the existing frame tick so no extra timer), emits level changes via onIdleEscalationChange, and the controller mirrors them to re-label the animation badge Idle -> Impatient -> Frustrated. Escalation is codogotchi-pet only because the rows live on the lite sheet; the Codex pet keeps its plain idle animation (floatingFrames(forIdleEscalation:) returns [] and the renderer falls back).
prompt_lesson: Reserved assets plus a 'the renderer selects these' doc comment are not a feature — they are a TODO that reads as done. When sprite rows / fixtures are added ahead of the logic that drives them, the gap is invisible until someone tries to exercise it. A ticket that ships escalation art should either ship the selection logic or explicitly mark the rows as pending so a reviewer can see the wiring is absent. Second lesson: time-based UI behavior needs an injected clock and an env-overridable threshold from day one, both so it is unit-testable deterministically and so a human can watch minutes-long transitions in seconds.
test_reachability: Good. Pure units cover IdleEscalationConfig thresholds, env-override resolution (and invalid-input fallback), and badge labels. Scene-level tests use an injected clock to drive idle->impatient->frustrated, assert reset-on-transition and re-arm-on-return-to-idle, and assert the observer emission sequence. Final aesthetics (the actual impatient/frustrated sprite art and 5/10-min feel) remain a visual check, eased by the env override.

commit: 7bc00a4 fix(menubar): apply RPG HUD toggle live without an app restart
problem: Settings -> RPG -> 'Show RPG HUD' toggle did not take effect until the app was restarted. Deselecting it left the HUD visible; selecting it (when launched deselected) did not re-enable it — both only resolved on relaunch, which reads config fresh at startup. P10.08-B, routed to QC from the phase-10 advisory triage.
solution: The toggle handler only wrote rpg_hud_enabled to config and updated the tab view-model; nothing pushed the change to the running floating HUD. The HUD re-read the flag in exactly one place — the LivePollingDriver applyRPGState callback (MenubarApp.swift) — which is change-gated on RPG numeric deltas (half_hearts/levelFraction/level differ from last). With static RPG stats that callback never fires, so the hud_enabled flag was starved and only re-read at next launch. Fix adds the missing live-apply wire: SettingsWindowController exposes onRPGHUDEnabledChanged (fired with the *persisted* value, since setRPGHUDEnabled reverts on a failed write, so the live HUD tracks what survives relaunch); MenubarApp forwards it to FloatingPetController.setRPGHUDEnabled -> FloatingPetPanel.setRPGHUDEnabled, which flips RPGHUDViewModel.setHUDEnabled and re-runs the hide / hover-reveal logic immediately. setHUDEnabled is visibility-only — it leaves the last snapshot (hearts/ring/level) intact and emits no flash. Disable hides at once; enable restores the hover-driven reveal (HUD pops back on next hover, by existing design — it is not always-on). Note: this fixes only the write direction (toggle -> live HUD). The read direction half of P10.08-B (checkbox shows stale state on window reopen when config changed externally) is NOT addressed here and remains open.
prompt_lesson: Second occurrence of the codogotchi-01 round-1 pattern: a control signal piggybacked on a callback that fires only under a *different* trigger condition gets silently starved. codogotchi-01 hung bubble re-anchoring on a persist-on-mouseUp handler (fired only at drag end); here hud_enabled was re-read only inside a poll callback gated on RPG-value deltas (fires only when stats change). Transferable attack: for any setting/flag that must affect a running view, trace the *single* code path that re-reads it at runtime and ask 'under what condition does that path execute?' If that condition is unrelated to the setting changing (a delta gate, a mouseUp, a periodic-but-conditional emit), the setting is starved whenever that condition is absent. A control signal must ride a path triggered by the signal's own change, not be a passenger on an unrelated change-gated emit. Corollary specific to settings UI: persisting to config is not applying — a toggle that writes config needs an explicit live-apply call into the running view, distinct from whatever reads config at startup.
test_reachability: Mixed. The leaf units are cheap and now covered: controller forwards the toggle to the panel (FloatingPetPanelSpy), and view-model setHUDEnabled flips visibility without disturbing the snapshot or flashing. But the *integration* gap — that the only runtime reader of hud_enabled was change-gated, so a passing 'flipping it off hides the HUD' acceptance test (ticket-08 line 16) could drive applyRPGState itself and mask the starvation — is not reachable by a pure unit. The ticket's acceptance criterion was weaker than its requirement (line 11 said 'without restart'; line 16 only said 'flipping it off hides the HUD'), so a green test never proved the live-apply requirement. Catching this class needs a test that asserts the toggle path reaches the HUD with NO intervening RPG poll, which the new controller-forwarding test now approximates.

commit: 54598e8 fix(xp): skip historical tokens on fresh install; fix tombstone centering
problem: On a clean Codogotchi install (no .local-xp-cache.json), defaultCache() initialises last_read_at_claude and last_read_at_codex to null. parseSince(null) resolves to new Date(0) — Unix epoch, 1970-01-01. The first hook fire for each source therefore scans ALL historical JSONL since the beginning of time, dumping the user's entire pre-existing token history as XP in one shot. The two cursors are independent, so two separate level jumps occur: first Codex hook (a cat-facts prompt) imported all historical Codex tokens (lvl 1 → 18); first Claude hook (next conversation) imported all historical Claude tokens (lvl 18 → 35). Discovered by dogfooding a clean install and observing the level jump.
solution: When lastRead is null (first-ever run for that source), initialise the cursor to now and skip the scan. Future tokens accumulate from install day forward. Updated hook-binary.test.ts to pre-seed the cache with a cursor positioned just before the fixture event so the tests exercise the incremental-read path (the meaningful contract) rather than validating the epoch-dump behaviour.
prompt_lesson: A cursor/bookmark field initialised to null as 'never seen' must be guarded at its read site. When parseSince(null) silently resolves to epoch, null means 'import all history' — a one-time catastrophic import that is invisible in normal operation thereafter. Attack surface to add to adversarial review: for any append-only log reader that uses a cursor to bound its read window, trace the null/missing-cursor code path and ask 'what does this read on first install?' The test gap compounded it: the fixture seeded JSONL with past-timestamped events and the tests asserted that first-run imported them — the tests validated the epoch-dump behaviour as correct, masking the bug entirely. When tests exercise a default-state (null cursor) code path, verify that the default is the intended production behaviour, not an artifact of implementation.
test_reachability: Good. The incremental-read path is fully testable by pre-seeding the cache with a cursor before the fixture events (now done). The first-run skip is also directly testable: call runHook with no cache file and assert level stays at 1. The original tests only exercised the epoch-read path, making the bug look like validated correct behaviour.

commit: 54598e8 fix(xp): skip historical tokens on fresh install; fix tombstone centering
problem: ea88556 (style(hud): fill empty hearts and adjust tombstone size/alignment) doubled the tombstone from ringDiameter to ringDiameter*2 and changed the vertical y formula from an explicit ringCenterY computation (ringCenterY = petFrame.maxY - m.inset - m.heartHeight - m.rowGap - m.ringDiameter/2; y = ringCenterY - side/2) to a simplified top-of-hearts-row anchor (y = petFrame.maxY - m.inset - side). The doc comment still said 'a ringDiameter-sized square'; the tests still asserted tomb.width == m.ringDiameter (not 2×) and tomb.midY == ringCenterY — which the new y formula no longer satisfied. Both failures were latent since ea88556: no CI run was triggered after that commit. The 20% ring diameter increase for the XP hover feature (cefe352) made the magnitude large enough to appear as hard failures on the next CI run.
solution: Restored the correct vertical centering formula (ringCenterY from the pre-ea88556 code, then y = ringCenterY - side/2) so tombstone.midY aligns with ring.midY. Updated test assertions to expect m.ringDiameter * 2 for width and height.
prompt_lesson: When a diff changes a named size constant (let side = ringDiameter → ringDiameter*2), all three parallel representations must update atomically: the implementation, any doc comment describing it, and the test assertions pinning its value. A test asserting a concrete expected value that was NOT touched in the same diff that changed the underlying computation is a false green — it passes only because nobody ran it. Attack surface: for any diff touching a dimension, threshold, or named constant, grep for that constant in tests and comments; if either is unchanged while the formula changed, flag the divergence.
test_reachability: Good. tombstoneFrame is a pure function; size and centering assertions are directly testable and now passing. Discovery latency is the real lesson: a CI gate should have run after ea88556 landed. The fix is self-guarding — tests now pin the 2x size explicitly.

commit: c7e3ec8 fix(xp): clamp heal credit to one active-minute per wall-clock minute
problem: In packages/cli/src/local-xp-writer.ts, computeAndPersistV5Fields ran cache.active_minutes += 1 once per hook invocation. But the heal contract ACTIVE_MINUTES_PER_HALF_HEART=60 and the engine resolveHalfHearts using floor(activeMinutes/60) both treat the unit as a wall-clock minute. The result: a half-heart healed every 60 hook EVENTS, not 60 minutes of coding. Heal rate became a function of tool-call frequency (a fast burst of edits could heal in minutes; sparse work took much longer) instead of time actually spent coding. Surfaced while reasoning through the heal mechanics during the floating-pet decay discussion (the symptom that opened the thread was the unrelated unwired Swift decay timer; this was found by inspecting the writer).
solution: Gate the increment to at most one active-minute per rolling 60s window. Added a persisted last_active_credit_at cursor to LocalXpCache (backfilled to null on read so existing caches migrate cleanly); only increment active_minutes when >=60_000ms have elapsed since the last credited event, then advance the cursor. Rolling-window, not calendar-minute bucketing, so events straddling a minute boundary cannot double-credit within seconds. last_activity_at still updates on every event from all five platforms (decay baseline + keep-hearts-alive); only the heal credit is gated. Added a test firing three events inside one minute (active_minutes==1) plus one at +60s (==2).
prompt_lesson: The P10.05 subagent review looked directly at this hunk and recorded surface result #4: 'the active_minutes % 60 logic is arithmetically sound ... even if active_minutes somehow reached 120, the code would consistently award two heals.' It validated the modulo/division arithmetic while accepting the counter's unit without question. The miss: it checked 'does the arithmetic work' instead of 'does one increment equal one minute.' Transferable attack surface: for ANY accumulator that is later divided by a constant named <UNIT>_PER_<THING> (here ACTIVE_MINUTES_PER_HALF_HEART), trace the `+=` site and confirm a single increment advances by exactly one <UNIT>. `x += 1` per event where x is labeled in minutes and the comment says 'active coding minutes' is a unit conflation that passes every arithmetic check. An accumulator's NAME is a contract about its unit; the increment cadence must honor it.
test_reachability: Good. Directly unit-testable: fire N hook events within a 60s window and assert active_minutes increments by 1, then one event past +60s asserts the next credit. Now covered. The original tests never asserted active_minutes after multiple same-window events — the same review's surface #12 explicitly noted 'no test for non-zero active_minutes carry-forward,' so the gap was visible in the review's own notes but not connected to the unit bug.

commit: 9d5e246f fix(developer-tab): read state.d/ slices instead of deprecated state.json
problem: After Phase 12 the hook exclusively writes per-session slices via writeSliceAtomic — writeStateAtomic (state.json) is never called. DeveloperTabViewModel still read from stateJsonPath, so Settings > Developer showed a perpetual 'state.json: v6   renderer: v7' mismatch warning. Root cause: schema_version was also absent from SliceEntry (the contract type), so even if the ViewModel had read state.d/ it could not have inspected the version. Two gaps compounded: wrong read target AND missing field on the contract.
solution: Added schema_version: z.literal(STATE_JSON_SCHEMA_VERSION) to sliceEntrySchema so every new slice carries its version at write time. Updated hook-binary.ts to include schema_version in the slice construction. Overhauled DeveloperTabViewModel: stateDirPath replaces stateJsonPath; new latestSlicePath computed property finds the most-recently-modified .json slice via mtime (filtering .tmp- partials); stateSchemaVersion and stateJsonPretty read from that slice. Updated SettingsWindowController to pass state.d/ path and updated display labels. All tests updated; Swift suite 0 failures, TS at pre-existing 2-failure baseline.
prompt_lesson: When a phase migrates the canonical write target (state.json → state.d/), every reader must be enumerated and updated atomically or the old path becomes a stale artifact that silently returns wrong data. The Developer tab was missed because it was purely observational and not on the feature hot-path. Attack surface: after any write-target migration, grep for the old path name across ALL consumers — not just the hook and renderer, but diagnostics, status tabs, and test helpers — and update each one in the same commit. A contract type (SliceEntry) that lacks a version field cannot be validated; schema_version should have been added to SliceEntry when state.d/ was introduced in Phase 12.
test_reachability: Good post-fix. DeveloperTabViewModelTests now exercises makeStateDir (creates state.d/ with a slice), schemaVersionMismatch for match/mismatch/non-integer/absent cases, and pretty-print presence. Pre-fix there were no tests for the stale state.json read path because the mismatch only manifested at runtime against live disk state.

commit: 9a9fbd56 fix(p12-qc): fix firingRecently, dismissAttention, drop state.json shim
problem: Three Phase-12 regressions discovered while auditing which code still referenced state.json after codogotchi-14 was landed. (1) hooks.ts hooksStatus() called readStateJson() to compute firingRecently and last_event_at per platform. Since state.json is never written post-P12, firingRecently was always false and last_event_at was always null for every platform — the hook-status display in Settings > General was permanently stale. (2) StateJsonWriter.dismissAttention received config.pollingTarget.path which is now the state.d/ directory, but treated it as a single-file path, called Data(contentsOf:) on a directory, and silently returned on the guard-let failure — attention dismissal (clearing the attention bubble on user interaction so it does not reappear on relaunch) was permanently broken. (3) status.ts runStatus had a conscious 'fall back to legacy state.json if no slices' shim from the P12 transition window. That window has closed; the shim was dead code on any system with hooks installed.
solution: (1) Replaced readStateJson in hooks.ts with readLatestSliceForHooks, which reads state.d/, parses slices via sliceEntrySchema.safeParse, and returns the most-recent winner by updated_at. Downstream updated to read origin from the slice's top-level field instead of source_event.origin. (2) StateJsonWriter.dismissAttention now iterates contentsOfDirectory on the dir path and patches each .json slice in-place (removing attention, setting activity_state idle), restoring the relaunch-clean behaviour. (3) Removed readStateJson, stateJsonPath, and the ternary shim from status.ts; removed both from exports (no external callers). Clean break.
prompt_lesson: codogotchi-14 fixed the most visible symptom (Developer tab mismatch) but did not enumerate ALL state.json readers. The same migration audit that caught the ViewModel missed three other call sites: hooksStatus, dismissAttention, and the runStatus shim. Lesson: a write-target migration audit must be exhaustive and machine-verified — grep for the old path constant or function name across the entire codebase before closing the migration ticket, not just in the files touched by the primary fix. A partial audit produces a partial fix and leaves a class of bugs open. Secondary lesson for dismissAttention specifically: a method that 'fails silently' is invisible in testing and in logs — its silent failure masquerades as a behavior change in the surrounding feature (attention bubble reappearing on relaunch), which is misattributed to the calling code rather than the writer. Silent-fail helpers need integration tests that assert the side-effect actually occurred, not just that the method did not throw.
test_reachability: Mixed. firingRecently: fully testable by mocking the state.d/ directory and asserting the hooksStatus return. dismissAttention: testable by creating a temp state.d/ with a slice carrying attention, calling the method, and asserting the field is gone — no test currently exists for this path (silent-fail + no test = invisible regression). runStatus shim: pre-existing status.test.ts already covers the slice-read path; the shim removal does not change any passing test. Recommended follow-up: add a StateJsonWriterTests.swift that exercises dismissAttention against a real temp directory.

summary: Static phase-13 menubar icon was hard-coded to 18x18pt and rendered undersized next to system menu-bar icons.
problem: Phase-13 introduced a static menubar status-item icon by sizing NSApp.applicationIconImage to a fixed 18x18pt. macOS app-icon assets carry intrinsic transparent padding and a squircle inset, so at 18pt the visible mark was noticeably smaller than neighboring menu-bar icons (the system calendar icon, and a much larger third-party paw icon). The icon read as floating and undersized.
solution: Sized the status-item image to NSStatusBar.system.thickness instead of a hard-coded 18pt, so the app icon's own intrinsic padding supplies the breathing room and the mark reads at a weight comparable to its neighbors. Verified visually by the operator against the live menu bar.

fixCommit.subject: fix(p13-qc): size menubar status icon to bar thickness

reachability.evidence: Phase-13 shipped a static app-icon menubar image. The undersize is only visible by running the app and comparing against neighboring menu-bar icons; it is not present in the diff, the ticket spec, or any unit surface.
reachability.promptLesson: Menubar/status-item visual sizing must be dogfooded against real neighbors. A hard-coded point size that looks reasonable in code can render undersized because app-icon assets carry intrinsic padding the code does not account for. Prefer platform metrics (NSStatusBar.system.thickness) over magic numbers.

summary: Monochrome menu-bar setting rendered the app icon as a filled block because the full app icon was used as a template image.
problem: Phase-13's 'monochrome menu bar icon' toggle set isTemplate=true on NSApp.applicationIconImage. macOS template images render only the alpha channel in the system tint, and the full app icon's alpha is a solid rounded square — so monochrome mode showed a filled block (white when the menu was active) rather than a recognizable icon. The defect was known and deliberately deferred when codogotchi-16 fixed the sizing of the same icon, then fixed here.
solution: Monochrome mode now renders a grayscale copy of the same app icon (CIColorControls saturation=0, isTemplate=false), preserving shape and shading and removing only color, so the icon no longer changes form when the setting is toggled. Mirrors the existing MenubarRenderer.desaturate path and falls back to the color icon if CGImage bridging fails. Operator considered and rejected a pet-silhouette template (changed the icon shape on toggle) before settling on desaturation.

fixCommit.subject: fix(p13-qc): render menubar icon in grayscale for monochrome mode

reachability.evidence: Only visible by toggling the monochrome setting and viewing the live menu bar (and its active/selected state). Not present in the diff, the ticket spec, or any unit surface.
reachability.promptLesson: A macOS template image renders only the alpha channel, so a full-color/opaque asset (an app icon) can never be a template — it collapses to a filled block. Choose template-vs-fixed-image by the asset’s alpha, and dogfood every menu-bar visual state (color, monochrome, and selected) because none are unit-reachable. A monochrome toggle should desaturate, not re-silhouette, unless a purpose-built glyph exists.

summary: Attention-bubble dismiss/focus did not persist in multi-pet mode, so the bubble re-appeared on the next poll tick for every per-platform pet.
problem: Phase-13's p13.04 FloatingPetWindowPool refactor replaced the single floatingPetPanelController with a per-origin window factory but dropped the onAttentionDismissed wiring that the single-window path had. As a result, handleBubbleDismiss() flipped the pet to idle in memory and called a nil onAttentionDismissed closure — nothing was written to state.d/. On the next 1 Hz poll, FloatingPetWindowPool re-read the still-present attention payload from the slice and re-showed the bubble. Because the dismiss never persisted, the bug affected every per-platform floating pet: clicking dismiss (x) or Focus appeared to idle the pet for a frame, then the bubble immediately returned.
solution: Re-wired panel.onAttentionDismissed in the pool factory to call StateJsonWriter.dismissAttention against config.pollingTarget.path (the state.d/ directory). Added an optional origin filter to dismissAttention: in multi-pet mode the clear is scoped to the dismissed window's origin (match on source_event.origin) so dismissing one pet does not silence pending attention on the others; the shared 'combined' window passes nil to clear all slices, matching its aggregate winner semantics. Added StateJsonWriterTests coverage asserting a scoped dismiss leaves a different origin's attention untouched.

fixCommit.subject: fix(p13-qc): persist attention-bubble dismiss per origin in multi-pet mode

reachability.evidence: The dropped onAttentionDismissed wiring is not visible in any unit surface: the panel-level handleBubbleDismiss and the StateJsonWriter both had passing tests in isolation. The regression only manifests by running the app, dismissing a live bubble, and waiting one or more poll ticks to see it return — a dogfood-only interaction across the panel -> state.d/ -> pool re-read loop.
reachability.promptLesson: A large refactor that swaps a single owner for a factory/pool must re-audit every callback the old owner wired. Grep the deleted owner for each `.on<Event> =` assignment and confirm each is re-established (or deliberately dropped) in the new path. A silent-fail helper (dismissAttention returns void, fails quietly) makes a missing caller invisible: the feature looks broken in the calling layer, not the helper. Wiring presence is itself a behavior — assert the side effect (state.d/ slice mutated) end-to-end, not just that each unit works alone.

testReachability: The writer is fully unit-testable (temp state.d/, assert slice mutated/untouched per origin) and now is. The missing wiring itself is not unit-reachable in practice — it lives in the MenubarApp pool factory closure that needs a live NSPanel/NSStatusBar and a running poll loop. An integration/dogfood pass is the realistic guard for the closure being connected.

summary: The 'Dismiss after idle: N minutes' setting had no effect — a present-but-idle floating pet never dismissed because the TTL clock was reset every poll tick.
problem: FloatingPetWindowPool set lastSeenAt[origin] = currentTime on every tick an origin was present in the snapshot (Step 2), and the idle-dismiss TTL was measured as currentTime - lastSeenAt. Because an idle agent's slice lingers in state.d/ (the reader keeps slices for ~2h), the origin stayed present every poll and lastSeenAt refreshed to now each tick, so currentTime - lastSeenAt was ~0 forever. The TTL therefore measured 'time since the slice left state.d/' (i.e. tool switch/quit), NOT 'time the pet has been idle' as the spec and the Settings UI promise ('Dismiss after idle: 1 minute'). Result: a finite TTL behaved identically to 'Never' for any still-running tool — the feature was completely non-functional. The phase-13 acceptance scenario (implementation-plan.md:56, ticket-04) explicitly described 'leaving both tools idle causes the non-last-active window to dismiss within 60 seconds', but every unit test substituted an EMPTY snapshot to fake staleness, exercising slice-absence rather than the idle-present path the spec describes — so the gap was invisible to the test surface.
solution: Freeze the TTL clock while idle: lastSeenAt[origin] now only refreshes when activityState != .idle (seeded on first sight so a freshly-observed idle pet still gets a full TTL grace window before disappearing), so the clock accumulates idle duration. Factored a shared isTTLExpired(windowKey:) predicate (not-last-active AND now - lastSeen > ttl) and used it in Step 5b (dismiss) and as a spawn guard in Step 7 (own) and Step 8 (combined) — without the spawn guard, Step 5b would drop the window and the spawn loop would immediately re-create it from the lingering idle slice, so the pet would flicker but never disappear. Last-active immunity is preserved per spec (the most-recently-active window is never idle-dismissed; operator chose to keep this). Added testIdleOriginPastTTLIsDismissedWhileStillPresent and testActivityResetsIdleDismissClock; the pre-existing empty-snapshot TTL tests still pass, confirming the slice-absence path is intact.

fixCommit.subject: fix(p13-qc): measure idle-dismiss TTL from last activity, not slice presence

reachability.evidence: The defect is invisible on the static surfaces: the code reads as a plausible 'last-seen TTL', and every unit test triggered dismissal with an empty snapshot, so the present-but-idle path the spec actually describes was never executed. Surfacing it required running the app, setting a 1-minute TTL, leaving tools idle, and watching the pet fail to dismiss across many poll cycles — a real dogfood interaction over wall-clock time.
reachability.promptLesson: When an acceptance criterion is stated in terms of a real-world condition ('leave the tool idle'), the test must reproduce THAT condition, not a convenient proxy. Substituting an empty snapshot for 'idle' silently changes the property under test from 'idle pet dismisses' to 'absent pet dismisses' — they share a code path only by accident, and the one the user cares about went uncovered. For any time-based / TTL / debounce / staleness feature, identify exactly which signal advances the clock (presence vs. activity vs. wall-time) and write a test that holds the entity present-but-inactive across the threshold. A green TTL test that removes the entity to expire it is testing teardown, not the timeout.

testReachability: Fully unit-reachable once the right scenario is written — the pool takes an injectable now() and customization/snapshot doubles, so present-but-idle-across-TTL is directly expressible (the two added tests do exactly this). The gap was not tool reachability but scenario fidelity: the existing tests reproduced the wrong real-world condition (absent instead of idle).

summary: Selecting a different pet in Settings > Pet did not live-swap visible floating windows; the change only took effect on app restart or a window respawn.
problem: The p13.04 FloatingPetWindowPool refactor replaced the single floating-pet controller with a per-origin pool, but reloadActivePet() (the Settings > Pet activation path) was never wired to push the newly selected pet into the pool's existing windows. It updated the shared self.codexPet/self.codogotchiPet, the menubar status-icon renderer, and the polling driver — so newly spawned windows and a full app restart picked up the new pet, but any already-visible floating pet kept rendering the old one until it was dismissed and respawned. The regression was self-documented in the diff with the comment 'Pool-owned windows retain their existing pet until naturally respawned on next tick.', which framed a silently-dropped pre-refactor behavior (live pet swap) as intended.
solution: Added replacePets(codexPet:codogotchiPet:) to FloatingPetWindowControlling and FloatingPetPanelManaging (the concrete FloatingPetPanelController already implemented it; a default no-op in the protocol extension keeps test stubs conforming). FloatingPetController forwards it to its panel; FloatingPetWindowPool.replacePets broadcasts it to every live window; reloadActivePet now calls the pool broadcast instead of carrying the resigned comment. Newly spawned windows continue to pick up the new pet via the factory-captured refs. Added testReplacePetsBroadcastsToEveryActiveWindow and patched two other stub conformers.

fixCommit.subject: fix(p13-qc): live-swap pet in pool windows on Settings pet change

reachability.evidence: The defect was visible on the static review surface: the p13.04 diff added an explicit comment to reloadActivePet — 'Pool-owned windows retain their existing pet until naturally respawned on next tick.' — announcing that the live-swap path no longer reaches the floating windows. A reviewer needed no dogfooding; the diff itself documented the behavior change. The miss was accepting that rationalizing comment at face value rather than challenging whether the pre-refactor single-controller path swapped the visible pet eagerly (it did).
reachability.promptLesson: When a refactor ADDS a comment that announces a new limitation in the shape 'X no longer happens until Y' / 'retained until naturally respawned' / 'takes effect on next restart', treat it as a regression smell, not documentation. Ask whether the pre-refactor path did X eagerly; if so, the comment is describing a silently-dropped behavior. A self-documenting limitation in a diff is review-reachable evidence — challenge it instead of accepting the author's framing that it is intended. This is the diff-surface twin of the silent refactor-drop class: same root cause (a single-owner behavior not re-established in the new owner), but here the author left a written tell.

testReachability: Fully unit-reachable and now covered: the pool takes an injectable window factory, so a broadcast-reaches-every-window assertion is direct (testReplacePetsBroadcastsToEveryActiveWindow builds a CodexPet from the mali fixture and counts replacePets calls per stub). No live AppKit surface is required to guard the wiring.

summary: Hiding a pet via right-click or menubar respawned it after one poll tick; "Show Pet" was always disabled so there was no way to un-hide without restarting.
problem: FloatingPetWindowPool.setVisible(false) removed the window from windows[] but wrote no memory of user intent. On the next update() tick the origin was still present in visibleEntries, windows[origin]==nil, so Steps 7/8 re-spawned a fresh window — resetting the pet to its default spawn position. Compounding this, MenubarMenu.buildPetSection rendered "Show Pet" as disabled (action=nil) whenever activeOrigins was empty, so there was no interactive path to un-hide a pet without an app restart.
solution: Added userHiddenWindowKeys: Set<String> to FloatingPetWindowPool. setVisible(false) now inserts the key and removes the window; update() Steps 7 and 8 skip spawn for any key in userHiddenWindowKeys so the intent survives across ticks. setVisible(true) removes the key and re-spawn flows naturally on the next tick. Rewrote MenubarMenu.buildPetSection to handle the hidden-key set: one active+zero hidden stays as the existing single "Hide Pet" toggle; zero active+one hidden renders an enabled "Show Pet" wired to a new showFloatingPetForKey action; any mixed or multi-item state renders per-key "Hide X Pet" and "Show X Pet" items. Added 3 pool tests and 2 menu tests.

fixCommit.subject: fix(p13-qc): persist hide-pet across pool ticks; wire Show Pet action

reachability.evidence: The re-spawn only manifests by hiding a pet and watching the running app: the window disappears, the tick fires (~1s), and the pet reappears at the default bottom-left spawn corner. Not present in the diff, the ticket spec, or any unit surface — FloatingPetWindowPool.setVisible was a one-liner that looked correct in isolation.
reachability.promptLesson: When a user-facing action removes an item from a pool/registry that is fed by a continuously-present backing source (state.d/ snapshots), the pool must persist the user's intent separately — removing the window is not enough if the next tick will re-add it from the source. Attack surface: for any pool with a periodic update() that spawns from a live snapshot, ask "if setVisible(false) removes the window but the snapshot is still present, what does the next update() tick do?" A state bit tracking user-explicit-hide is the correct guard; TTL expiry is not — TTL fires for inactivity, not for a deliberate user action.

testReachability: Fully unit-reachable once the correct scenario is written. The pool takes an injectable snapshot and customization, so a hide-then-tick assertion is direct: call setVisible(false), then call update(snapshot) one or more times, then assert activeOrigins still excludes the hidden key. Three new pool tests cover this (own-mode, show-clears-flag, combined-mode). The menu tests add enabled-Show-Pet and mixed-state-list assertions. The re-spawn was only discovered by running the app and observing behavior.

summary: All floating pets spawned at the same bottom-left position on app load, hide/show cycles, and initial platform activation.
problem: MenubarApp.swift's window factory created every FloatingPetController with saveState: { _ in } (no-op) and no per-origin initial frame. Each controller independently called AppStateStore.load() — which reads a single global floating_pet.frame — so all pool windows got the same frame and positions were never written back to disk. On app load every active platform's pet appeared at the same coordinate; hiding and showing a pet respawned it at the same default spot.
solution: Schema v3 adds floating_pet_positions: { origin: frame } to app-state.json. AppStateStore gains loadFrame(for:visibleFrame:) and saveFrame(_:for:). FloatingPetController.init gains an optional initialState parameter so pool-created controllers bypass the global load. The pool factory in MenubarApp now loads the per-origin frame before construction and wires saveState to AppStateStore.saveFrame(_:for:origin). save(_:) reads and preserves any existing positions so hook-status refreshes (30s cadence) cannot clobber them. Five new AppStateTests cover the new load/save API.

fixCommit.subject: fix(p13-qc): persist per-origin floating-pet positions across sessions and hide/show cycles

reachability.evidence: Not present in any diff or spec surface. Requires running the app with two or more active platforms and observing that every pet window appears at the same screen coordinate. The root cause (saveState: { _ in }) looked intentional in isolation — suppressing persistence for pool controllers was a deliberate P13.04 authoring decision; only dogfooding revealed the user-visible consequence.
reachability.promptLesson: When a refactor replaces a single stateful owner with a pool, audit every piece of per-owner state (position, saved frame, visibility, etc.) and explicitly decide whether it should be global, per-owner, or discarded. saveState: { _ in } was used to suppress the unwanted global-visibility write, but it also silently discarded the per-owner frame. For each no-op override in a factory closure, ask: "Is this suppressing a harmful side-effect only, or am I also suppressing a necessary one?" Pool-spawned controllers need their own persistence scope, not no-op suppression.

testReachability: Fully unit-reachable once per-origin load/save API exists. Five new AppStateTests cover round-trip, preservation across origins, clobber-resistance, and offscreen clamping. The original bug was invisible to unit tests because all pool-controller tests used injectable saveState closures that never read from disk — the interaction between factory, pool, and disk state required a running app to manifest.

summary: Pool spawned own-mode windows lacked teardown on own<->minimalist mode switch, so Settings mode changes silently did nothing until TTL or restart.
problem: FloatingPetWindowPool.update() had explicit teardown for own->off (Step 5a) and own->combined (Step 6a) transitions, but no teardown for own<->minimalist. Since ownOrigins (the filter that selects non-combined origins) includes both .own and .minimalist, when an origin's mode flipped, windows[origin] was already non-nil with the wrong controller type, so the `if windows[origin] == nil` spawn gate in Step 7 was never re-entered and the stale window kept receiving apply() calls under the new mode. Switching Own -> Minimalist in Settings appeared to do nothing unless an AttentionBubble happened to be showing, in which case the separate AttentionBubblePanel (a compact horizontal strip) was mistaken for the minimalist strip actually working.
solution: Added windowSpawnedModes: [String: PlatformMode] to FloatingPetWindowPool, recorded at spawn time. Added Step 6b: for any ownOrigins window whose spawnedMode no longer matches the current mode, tear it down before the Step 7 spawn gate runs, so the correct factory (minimalistWindowFactory vs windowFactory) is invoked on the same tick. Cleaned up the tracking dict in every existing dismiss path (5a off-mode, 5b TTL-stale, 6a own->combined, idle-past-TTL guard, setVisible(false)) so it never holds a stale entry for a removed window.

fixCommit.subject: fix(menubar): tear down stale window on own<->minimalist mode switch

reachability.promptLesson: When a pool/factory keys windows by origin and routes construction on a mode enum (off/own/combined/minimalist), every pairwise mode transition needs explicit teardown, not just the ones the ticket happened to exercise. own->off and own->combined were covered because earlier tickets needed them; own<->minimalist was added in a later ticket (P14.06) without auditing the full transition matrix against the now-larger mode enum. Lesson: when adding a new case to an enum that drives a switch/factory dispatch inside a stateful pool, enumerate the full N x N transition matrix against existing teardown steps, not just the spawn path for the new case.

testReachability: Good once written, but the original P14.06 ticket only added a pool test for minimalist spawning from a cold pool (testMinimalistOriginUsesMinimalistFactoryAndLifecycleParity) and never a same-origin own->minimalist or minimalist->own re-tick test, so the missing teardown path had zero coverage. Added testOwnToMinimalistTransitionReplacesWindow and testMinimalistToOwnTransitionReplacesWindow to FloatingPetWindowPoolTests.swift asserting the correct factory fires on the second tick after a mode change. Verified manually in the running app: Settings -> Pet -> switching Codex from Own to Minimalist now replaces the window immediately without requiring an attention bubble.

summary: Combined window showed Star badge during non-idle states instead of the active platform badge.
problem: Phase-14 added the persistent Star/Default badge for the combined window while idle (Step 8, FloatingPetWindowPool). The idle branch called applyPlatform(origin: "combined"), but there was no else branch for non-idle states. Own-mode windows (Step 7) call applyPlatform with state.sourceEvent?.origin regardless of idle/active. The combined window never mirrored this: when the winning platform was Thinking, Waiting for Input, etc., applyPlatform went uncalled and the last-set badge (the Star from the previous idle tick) persisted visually.
solution: Added an else-if branch in Step 8 after the idle guard: when activityState != .idle and winner.sourceEvent?.origin is non-nil, call applyPlatform with that origin. Matches the per-platform behavior own-mode windows had before phase-13. The idle Star badge is preserved.

fixCommit.subject: fix(menubar): badge combined window with active platform when not idle

reachability.evidence: Only visible by running the app with a combined pet in a non-idle state (e.g. Thinking, Waiting for Input) and observing whether the platform badge updates. The idle badge was correct (screenshots confirmed). The non-idle miss is not present in the diff, the ticket spec, or any unit surface — Step 8 called applyPlatform in one branch and was silent in the other, which reads as plausible in isolation.
reachability.promptLesson: When a parallel code path (combined-window Step 8) is adapted from a sibling path (own-mode Step 7) to add a special-case branch (idle → Star badge), check that the sibling's other branches are also carried over. "Special case added" and "remaining branches preserved" are two separate review checks. No test currently verifies that Step 8 calls applyPlatform with winner.sourceEvent?.origin for non-idle states — the badge routing was untested. A direct test would: build a combined snapshot with an active winner (activityState == .thinking, sourceEvent.origin == "claude_code"), call update(), and assert applyPlatform was called with "claude_code".

summary: Pet tab description gap varied by card type, assign dropdown closed after each selection, and badge pills showed text names instead of platform icons.
problem: Three linked visual bugs in the Settings > Pet tab. (1) Description gap: `nameRow` height was driven by its tallest subview — 20pt when the assign button was present (installed pets), ~17pt when only the nameLabel (not-installed pets). Since `descLabel.topAnchor = nameRow.bottomAnchor + 4`, the description started 3pt lower on installed-pet cards, making same-row cards look misaligned. (2) Multiselect: The assign button opened an NSMenu via `menu.popUp(positioning:at:in:)`, which closes immediately after each item tap. The user had to re-click the assign button for every additional platform assignment. (3) Icon-only pills: Badge pills used text labels (`makeBadge(text:tint:)`) showing "Claude Code", "VS Code" etc. The user requested compact icon-only pills to reduce card size.
solution: (1) Added `nameRow.heightAnchor.constraint(greaterThanOrEqualToConstant: 20).isActive = true` so cards without an assign button maintain the same 20pt nameRow height, normalising the description Y position. (2) Replaced NSMenu with NSPopover (`PetAssignPopoverController`): a transient popover with a vertical list of platform rows (`BadgeRowView`); each row toggles in-place without closing the popover. The popover auto-dismisses on outside click via `.behavior = .transient`; `NSPopoverDelegate.popoverDidClose` triggers `reloadEntries()` to rebuild the grid with updated pills. (3) Replaced `makeBadge(text:tint:)` with `makePlatformIconPill(key:)` — a 22×18pt rounded container holding a 12×12pt NSImageView tinted via `contentTintColor`. Each popover row shows the platform SVG logo (from the asset catalog via `PlatformAttribution`) to the left of the platform name label.

fixCommit.subject: fix(menubar): pet tab layout, multiselect assign popover, icon-only pills

reachability.evidence: All three bugs required running the Settings > Pet tab to observe: the description gap is only visible when comparing installed and not-installed cards side by side; the NSMenu close-on-tap requires interacting with the dropdown; the text pills are a visual UX preference that reads as functional code in isolation.

For assignment controls that allow multiple values, verify the picker stays open across selections before shipping — NSMenu is a single-select primitive. Icon-only affordances should be verified against the asset catalog to confirm the correct template images resolve at runtime.
